title: The contribution of cannabis use to variation in the incidence of psychotic disorder across Europe (EU-GEI): A multicentre case-control study

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether, or how much, cannabis use causes psychotic disorders such as schizophrenia. The association with later psychosis is consistent and stronger with frequent use (see the answer on how often people use), but in the studies read a substantial part of it is explained by measured confounders, and genetically informed studies suggest that a further part reflects shared family or genetic liability, or genetic liability to schizophrenia making cannabis use more likely; none of these designs excludes a causal contribution, and none measures the effect of frequent or high-potency use. Adjustment for each cohort's measured confounders removed on average about 45% (10% to 80%) of the crude excess odds in seven cohorts (Moore et al., 2007). In the one co-relative study, a Swedish registry analysis described in a viewpoint whose second author co-wrote it (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), the odds ratio for schizophrenia with registry-recorded cannabis misuse fell from 10.44 in the general population to 5.07 in full siblings and to 3.52 (3.92 in the viewpoint's table) in identical twins discordant for misuse, with no significance test at the twin level and the adjustment set not stated. Three two-sample Mendelian randomization studies used genetic variants for having ever used cannabis, which explain about 1% or less of the variation in ever use where this is reported, with no adjustment beyond the source studies in the main analyses. The odds ratio for schizophrenia by genetic liability to ever use was 1.04 (95% CI 1.01 to 1.07) per doubling of the odds of ever use and 1.01 (0.93 to 1.10) by the pleiotropy-robust MR-Egger method (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02 to 1.14) per unit of log odds, which its authors rescale to 1.37 for ever against never use (Vaucher et al., 2018); and 1.04 (p = 0.81) with five genome-wide significant variants or 1.10 (0.99 to 1.21) with 69 variants (Pasman et al., 2018). In the reverse direction, genetic liability to schizophrenia was associated with ever using cannabis (1.10, 1.05 to 1.14, per doubling, Gage et al., 2017; 1.16, 1.06 to 1.27, per unit of log odds, Pasman et al., 2018), and the genetic correlation between ever use and schizophrenia was 0.25 (Pasman et al., 2018, as corrected). These three studies share consortium data and are not independent. Narrative reviews read the evidence available to them as shared vulnerability (Ksir & Hart, 2016), as partly causal with an appreciable non-causal share (Gillespie & Kendler, 2021), or as strong enough for a public-health message that cannabis can increase the risk (Gage et al., 2016; Murray et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: contested.
claims.magnitude: Not estimable as a causal effect. Attenuation of the crude association by each cohort's adjustment: about 45% on average (10% to 80%) (Moore et al., 2007). Co-relative (one registry study, misuse): OR 10.44 in the general population, 5.07 in full siblings, 3.52 or 3.92 in discordant identical twins (untested). Mendelian randomization, liability to ever use on schizophrenia: 1.04 (1.01–1.07) per doubling of the odds, MR-Egger 1.01 (0.93–1.10), 12 variants 1.03 (0.99–1.08) (Gage et al., 2017); 1.08 (1.02–1.14) per unit of log odds, rescaled 1.37 (1.09–1.67) ever vs never, 1.41 (1.09–1.83) adjusted for the variants' associations with ever smoking (Vaucher et al., 2018); 1.04 (p = 0.81) with 5 variants, 1.10 (0.99–1.21) with 69, GSMR 1.21 (p = 0.017) (Pasman et al., 2018). Liability to schizophrenia on ever use: 1.10 (1.05–1.14) per doubling (Gage et al., 2017); 1.16 (1.06–1.27) per unit (Pasman et al., 2018). Genetic correlation rg 0.25 (SE 0.03).

claims.statement: In general-population cohorts followed over time and in first-episode case-control studies, people who use cannabis, compared with people who do not, are more likely to develop psychotic symptoms or a psychotic disorder, and the association is stronger with more frequent use; no source read gives absolute risks by level of use. As a base rate, 362 of 50,087 men conscripted in Sweden in 1969 (about 7 in 1,000, editors' calculation) were diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, whatever their cannabis use (as tabulated in a narrative review, Gage et al., 2016). A systematic review of seven cohorts published to 2006 (Moore et al., 2007; AMSTAR 2 low confidence) pooled each cohort's own adjusted odds ratio (about 60 confounders across the studies, among them other substance use, personality traits, intellectual ability and other mental health problems): 1.41 (95% CI 1.20 to 1.65; I² 19%) for any later psychotic outcome, mostly self-reported or interview-rated symptoms, after ever use against never use; 2.09 (1.54 to 2.84; I² 44%) for each cohort's most frequent use (from more than 50 lifetime occasions to weekly or daily use or dependence) against no use, three of the six estimates not adjusted for other drug use; and 2.58 (1.08 to 6.13; I² 67%) for a psychotic disorder after ever use in the three cohorts with that outcome, or 1.82 (1.01 to 3.30) without the most heterogeneous one. Adjustment removed on average about 45% of the crude excess odds (10% to 80% by cohort). Of three cohorts published after that review, as summarized by Gage et al. (2016), the association did not remain after adjustment in two (Zurich; ALSPAC, 1.12, 0.76 to 1.65, after adjustment for tobacco and other illicit drugs), while a Californian hospital cohort reported a hazard ratio of 8.16 (5.08 to 13.12) for later admission with schizophrenia after a hospital diagnosis of cannabis use disorder, against people admitted with appendicitis. A meta-analysis of crude counts from ten studies (Marconi et al., 2016; AMSTAR 2 critically low) found the odds of a psychosis-related outcome rising with rank on each study's own scale of use, to 3.90 (2.84 to 5.34; I² 82%) at the top rank against never use, with nothing adjusted and with category-level odds that did not rise steadily in several studies. In two first-episode case-control studies from one team, daily use was reported more often by people with a psychotic disorder than by controls: fully adjusted odds ratio 3.2 (2.2 to 4.1) against never or occasional use (901 cases and 1,237 population controls at 11 sites in Europe and Brazil; adjusted for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco and other drugs; Di Forti et al., 2019) and 3.04 against never use (410 inpatients and 370 controls recruited by advertisement in south London; adjusted also for alcohol; Di Forti et al., 2015), whereas occasional use was not associated (0.84 and 0.96 for low- and high-potency types at the 11 sites; 0.58 for less-than-weekly use in south London) and ever use only weakly (1.3, 1.1 to 1.6) or not at all (0.93). Whether starting young adds risk beyond the amount used was not shown: the cohort review found no robust evidence that it does (Moore et al., 2007), and at the 11 sites first use at 15 or younger had a fully adjusted odds ratio of 1.6 (1.1 to 2.1) while the daily-use estimate changed little (3.1) when age at first use was added. The reviews give absolute figures only as calculations that assume the association is causal: a doubling from about 7 to 14 in 1,000 with regular use (Hall, 2015) and a lifetime risk of schizophrenia of about 2% with regular use (Gage et al., 2016). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
claims.magnitude: Moore et al. 2007 (7 cohorts; random-effects pooling of each cohort's adjusted odds ratio): any psychotic outcome, ever vs never use, 1.41 (1.20–1.65), I² 19.2%; most frequent use vs none, 2.09 (1.54–2.84), I² 44.1% (1.92, 1.50–2.47, without NEMESIS); psychotic disorder, ever use, 3 cohorts, 2.58 (1.08–6.13), I² 66.9% (1.82, 1.01–3.30, without NEMESIS); adjustment attenuated crude estimates by about 45% on average (10% to 80%). Later cohorts as summarized by Gage et al. 2016: ALSPAC 1.12 (0.76–1.65) after full adjustment; Zurich lost after adjustment; California HR 8.16 (5.08–13.12). Marconi et al. 2016 (10 studies, 66,816 people, crude counts): OR 3.90 (2.84–5.34) at the top rank vs never use, I² 82%. Di Forti et al. 2019 (901 cases, 1,237 controls; fully adjusted): daily use vs never or occasional 3.2 (2.2–4.1); more than once a week 1.4 (1.0–2.0); occasional use vs never 0.84 (low potency) and 0.96 (high potency); ever use 1.3 (1.1–1.6); first use at 15 or younger 1.6 (1.1–2.1). Di Forti et al. 2015 (410 cases, 370 controls; adjusted): every day 3.04 (printed 1.91–7.76), weekends 1.04, less than weekly 0.58 (0.25–1.32), ever use 0.93 (0.67–1.52). Base rate: Swedish conscripts, 362 of 50,087 diagnosed with schizophrenia by about age 45, about 7 in 1,000 (editors' calculation; all levels of use). Illustrations assuming causality: 7 rising to 14 in 1,000 with regular use (Hall, 2015); about 2% lifetime risk with regular use (Gage et al., 2016).

claims.statement: In two case-control studies from one research team, people presenting with a first episode of psychosis, compared with controls from the same areas, more often reported having mainly used high-potency cannabis, most of all daily, while mainly using low-potency cannabis was not associated with psychosis; potency was assigned from the type of cannabis people named, not measured. In south London (410 inpatients aged 18 to 65 with first-episode psychosis, 2005 to 2011, and 370 controls recruited by advertisement; Di Forti et al., 2015), 53% of patients and 19% of controls said they had mostly used skunk-like cannabis, and 14% and 44% hash-like cannabis; against people who had never used cannabis, adjusted odds ratios (for age, gender, ethnic origin, tobacco, alcohol, other drugs, education and employment) were 2.91 (printed 95% CI 1.52 to 3.60) for mainly skunk-like use and 0.83 (0.52 to 1.77) for mainly hash-like use, and 5.40 (2.80 to 11.30) for daily skunk-like use against 0.91 for daily hash-like use; several printed intervals do not fit their estimates or p-values, and the controls' exposure is printed in two versions that cannot both be right. At 11 sites in the UK, the Netherlands, France, Spain, Italy and Brazil (901 people with first-episode psychosis and 1,237 population controls, 2010 to 2015; Di Forti et al., 2019), where a type counted as high potency if its national mean THC was 10% or more, 37.1% of cases and 19.4% of controls reported mainly high-potency use; fully adjusted odds ratios against never use (for age, gender, ethnicity, education, employment, tobacco and other drugs) were 1.6 (1.2 to 2.2) for mainly high-potency and 1.1 (0.9 to 1.5) for mainly low-potency use, 1.5 (1.1 to 2.6) for high-potency use after also adjusting for daily use, and 4.78 (2.5 to 6.3) for daily high-potency use against 2.19 (1.4 to 3.6) for daily low-potency use, while occasional use of either kind was not associated (0.96 and 0.84); site estimates for high-potency use ranged from 0.6 to 3.6 without significant variation between sites. Both studies recorded cannabis type from recall after the illness began, measured no THC or cannabidiol, share investigators and the London catchment, and give attributable fractions for high-potency use (24% and 12.2%) that assume the associations are causal; the 24% cannot be reproduced from its printed inputs. A narrative review from the same group reports that schizophrenia polygenic scores did not differ between people using low- and high-potency cannabis (as described by Murray et al., 2016), whereas another review judged it too early to assume that only high-potency cannabis carries risk, because studies from before it was widespread also found an association, and asked that people selecting the extremes of use for other reasons be considered (Gage et al., 2016); the cohorts pooled to 2006 recorded how often people used, not what they used (Moore et al., 2007). Certainty: very low. Status: replicated by the same team.
claims.magnitude: Di Forti et al. 2015 (410 cases, 370 controls; adjusted): mainly skunk-like 2.91 (1.52–3.60 as printed), mainly hash-like 0.83 (0.52–1.77); daily skunk-like 5.40 (2.80–11.30), at weekends 2.70, less than weekly 1.90; daily hash-like 0.91, at weekends 0.62, less than weekly 0.49; mainly skunk-like use in 53% of patients and 19% of controls. Di Forti et al. 2019 (901 cases, 1,237 controls; fully adjusted): mainly high potency 1.6 (1.2–2.2), 1.5 (1.1–2.6) also adjusted for daily use; mainly low potency 1.1 (0.9–1.5); daily high potency 4.78 (2.5–6.3), daily low potency 2.19 (1.4–3.6), more than weekly 1.57 and 1.36, occasional 0.96 and 0.84; high-potency use in 37.1% of cases and 19.4% of controls; site-specific high-potency odds ratios 0.6 to 3.6 (variation by site p = 0.45). Attributable fractions assuming causality: high-potency use 24.0% (not reproducible from its inputs) and 12.2% (3.0–16.1).

claims.statement: Evidence is insufficient to say whether rates of schizophrenia or psychosis changed as cannabis use rose: the studies that narrative reviews cite disagree, all are ecological, and their figures are second-hand here. As described in the reviews, an Australian modelling study by the reviewers' own group found no clear rise in psychosis incidence after steep rises in cannabis use in the 1980s and 1990s; a British modelling study judged it too early to see any rise in England and Wales; case-register studies in Britain and Switzerland (south-east London and Zurich) reported rising incidence of psychoses in recent birth cohorts, and in south-east London incidence of schizophrenia was described as doubling between 1965 and 1999 while the share of patients who had used cannabis rose; a British study of people treated for schizophrenia in general practice found no increase, known only through a 2008 government advisory report (Hall & Degenhardt, 2009; Hall, 2015; Murray et al., 2016); and in the UK, according to a commentary cited by a critical overview, cannabis use rose at least tenfold since the 1970s without a rise in first admissions for schizophrenia, perhaps with a slight fall (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Reviews that lean towards a causal reading call this weak evidence: individuals' use and illness are not linked, confounders and other changing risk factors are not accounted for, even a causal effect would raise incidence only modestly, and changing diagnostic criteria, services and records could hide or create trends (Gage et al., 2016; Hall, 2015); the 2007 systematic review adds that time lags and unreliable incidence data may hide changes (Moore et al., 2007); the critical overview treats the UK figures as evidence against a causal effect (Ksir & Hart, 2016). Across places rather than over time, in one primary study of 10 sites in Europe and Brazil, adjusted incidence of psychotic disorder was higher where more controls reported daily use (r about 0.8) or high-potency use (about 0.7), an ecological correlation between two strongly overlapping measures (Di Forti et al., 2019). Certainty: very low. Status: mixed.
claims.magnitude: No pooled estimate. As described in reviews: no clear rise in Australia (modelling); too early to detect in England and Wales (modelling); rising incidence in recent birth cohorts in south-east London and Zurich (case registers), with schizophrenia incidence in south-east London described as doubling between 1965 and 1999; no rise in a British general-practice study (third-hand); at least a tenfold rise in UK cannabis use since the 1970s without a rise in first admissions (from a commentary). Across 10 sites: correlation of adjusted incidence with daily use among controls r = 0.8 (p = 0.0109) and with high-potency use r = 0.7 (p = 0.0286), the two exposures themselves strongly correlated.
